🤖 THREEHALVES — THE CENTAUR ROBOT Threehalves is a 7-foot-tall teleoperated robot developed by Satyress. Its design combines a human-like torso and arms with a powerful four-legged chassis, creating a mechanical centaur built for environments that are too dangerous for humans. The idea behind Threehalves is simple: instead of sending a person into extreme heat, unstable terrain, darkness, hazardous industrial environments or disaster zones, a skilled operator can control the robot remotely and perform the work from a safer location. Unlike many humanoid robots, Threehalves is designed around tools and equipment that humans already use. Its modular limbs and quick-connect system allow it to be adapted for different tasks, while its four-legged platform provides stability on difficult terrain. The most unsettling part is probably its appearance. With its enormous size, humanoid body, four mechanical legs and distinctive horned head, Threehalves looks less like a traditional industrial machine and more like something from a science-fiction horror movie. But behind the terrifying design is a serious engineering concept: putting the machine in danger instead of the human. Threehalves is still a developing robotics project, but it represents a strange glimpse into a future where dangerous jobs could be performed remotely — with a human controlling the machine from a distance. And honestly… it might be one of the creepiest robots ever built. 👁️ #threehalves #robot #baal #satyress #horrortok

XPeng’s humanoid robot IRON went viral after it fell during its first offline public demo at MixC Shenzhen Bay in Shenzhen on January 31, 2026. In videos from the event, IRON walks out with an eerily smooth, humanlike “model stride,” pauses near the center, and then—while raising an arm to the crowd—loses balance and faceplants. Staff reach in to steady it, but the robot still goes down and then has to be moved offstage by multiple people, which underlined just how heavy and non-human it really is.  The moment hit extra hard because IRON already had an “uncanny” reputation: XPeng has showcased it as a highly lifelike humanoid (even doing dramatic proof-of-it’s-not-a-person stunts during earlier reveals), and online skeptics had questioned whether the gait clips were real robotics.  XPeng’s CEO He Xiaopeng framed the fall as a normal development milestone—like a toddler learning to walk before it can run—and coverage noted subsequent demos using more support, hinting balance robustness is still a work in progress.

Visual artist Jason Cook  creates kinetic sculptures and robotic installations using electronics, programming and mechanical engineering. In The Walking Chair (2025), an ordinary wooden chair is transformed into a moving machine. A system of motors, mechanical parts and electronic components is attached beneath the seat, allowing the chair’s legs to move. By giving a familiar piece of furniture the ability to walk, Cook changes the way we perceive an everyday object. The chair is no longer simply something we sit on  it becomes an object with a movement of its own. #art #artist #weird #chair #avantgarde

A humanoid robot inside a Russian electronics store appeared to fight back after being pushed by a customer. CCTV footage shows the robot moving aggressively toward people inside the store, swinging its arms and kicking as several customers attempt to restrain it. The robot, nicknamed Sёma, had reportedly been introduced by the store as a humanoid “tech consultant” designed to interact with customers. What remains unclear is exactly what caused the response. There is currently no solid evidence confirming whether the robot was acting autonomously, following a programmed behaviour, being remotely controlled, or whether the incident was staged. Either way, footage of a humanoid robot physically clashing with people inside a store is a glimpse of a problem we may see far more often as robots enter public spaces. videos.caption: I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.
